from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Introduction: The Concept of a Moving Window", 
                          ["Discrete convolution is a sliding window operation.", 
                           "We use an input signal and a kernel.", 
                           "The kernel acts like a scanning lens."])
        
        signal = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.7, fill_opacity=0.3, fill_color=GRAY, stroke_color=WHITE) for _ in range(6)])
        signal.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0)
        self.place_in_area(signal, "B2", "B6")
        
        window = Square(side_length=0.7, fill_opacity=0.5, fill_color=YELLOW, stroke_color=YELLOW)
        window.move_to(signal[0])
        
        captured_values = Text("Captured", font_size=20, color=GREEN)
        self.place_at_grid(captured_values, "D4")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(signal))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(GRAY)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(window))
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(window.animate.move_to(signal[2]), run_time=1.5)
        self.play(FadeIn(captured_values))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN)
        self.wait(1)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Mechanics: Weighted Summation", [
            "Overlay the kernel onto the input grid.",
            "Multiply corresponding values element-wise.",
            "Sum the results to get a single output."
        ])
        
        # Create 3x3 input matrix
        input_matrix = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.8, color=WHITE) for _ in range(9)])
        input_matrix.arrange_in_grid(3, 3, buff=0)
        self.place_in_area(input_matrix, "A2", "C4", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        # Create 3x3 kernel matrix
        kernel_matrix = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.8, color="#00FFFF") for _ in range(9)])
        kernel_matrix.arrange_in_grid(3, 3, buff=0)
        self.place_in_area(kernel_matrix, "A2", "C4", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        self.play(Create(input_matrix))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.play(Create(kernel_matrix))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")
        # Highlighting pairs
        highlights = VGroup(*[SurroundingRectangle(m, color="#FF00FF", buff=0) for m in input_matrix])
        self.play(Create(highlights))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF4500")
        output_pixel = Square(side_length=0.8, color="#FF4500")
        self.place_at_grid(output_pixel, "E3", scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(FadeIn(output_pixel))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite Visual Intuition: Kernels as Filters", [
            "A kernel is just a matrix of numbers.", 
            "Blur filters average out the nearby pixel values.", 
            "Edge detection filters highlight sudden pixel changes."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # A kernel is just a matrix of numbers.
        matrix = Matrix([[1/9, 1/9, 1/9], [1/9, 1/9, 1/9], [1/9, 1/9, 1/9]])
        self.place_at_grid(matrix, 'B2', scale_factor=0.6)
        label1 = Text("Kernel (Blur)", font_size=20, color="#FFFFFF")
        label1.next_to(matrix, UP)
        self.add(matrix, label1)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Blur filters average out the nearby pixel values.
        # Simple representation of an averaging blur
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00BFFF"))
        blur_text = Text("Average", font_size=20, color="#00BFFF")
        blur_text.next_to(matrix, DOWN)
        self.add(blur_text)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Edge detection filters highlight sudden pixel changes.
        matrix_edge = Matrix([[-1, -1, -1], [-1, 8, -1], [-1, -1, -1]])
        self.place_at_grid(matrix_edge, 'E2', scale_factor=0.6)
        label2 = Text("Kernel (Edge)", font_size=20, color="#FFA500")
        label2.next_to(matrix_edge, UP)
        self.add(matrix_edge, label2)
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFA500"))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Applications: AI & Beyond", [
            "CNNs use multiple layers of learned convolutions.", 
            "Early layers detect simple lines and shapes.", 
            "Deeper layers combine features to recognize objects."
        ])
        
        # Objects
        # Layer visualization
        layer = VGroup(*[Rectangle(height=0.5, width=0.5, color=WHITE) for _ in range(9)]).arrange_in_grid(3, 3)
        self.place_at_grid(layer, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Kernel
        kernel = Square(side_length=0.5, color="#7FFF00", fill_opacity=0.3)
        self.place_at_grid(kernel, 'B2')
        
        # Feature Map
        feature_map = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.3, color="#FF1493", fill_opacity=0.5) for _ in range(4)]).arrange_in_grid(2, 2)
        self.place_at_grid(feature_map, 'E3', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.play(Create(layer))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#7FFF00"))
        self.play(
            kernel.animate.move_to(self.grid['B3']),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FF1493"))
        self.play(FadeIn(feature_map))
        self.wait(1)

outline.topic: Unlocking Discrete Convolutions: From Image Blurring to Feature Extraction
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Engineering

sections.title: Introduction: The Concept of a Moving Window (1 min)
sections.content: Define discrete convolution as a mathematical operation on two functions, focusing on the 'sliding window' approach. Introduce the two components: the Input Signal (the map) and the Kernel/Filter (the lens).
sections.example: Imagine a flashlight (the kernel) scanning over a pitch-black room (the signal) to reveal specific objects one by one.

sections.title: The Mechanics: Weighted Summation (1.5 mins)
sections.content: Explain the step-by-step process: overlay, multiply element-wise, and sum. Emphasize how the kernel 'weights' neighboring pixels. Use a 3x3 grid animation to show how a center pixel value changes based on its neighbors.
sections.example: A cat walking on a grid of numbered tiles; the cat's influence (kernel) is strongest on the tile it stands on and fades towards the adjacent ones.

sections.title: Prerequisite Visual Intuition: Kernels as Filters (1 min)
sections.content: Briefly review the prerequisite that a kernel is a matrix of numbers. Explain that changing these numbers changes the 'intent' of the convolution: smoothing (blurring) vs. sharpening (edge detection).
sections.example: Using a 'Blur' filter like a fogged-up window versus an 'Edge Detection' filter like a high-contrast ink sketch of a rabbit.

sections.title: Real-World Applications: AI & Beyond (1.5 mins)
sections.content: Connect the theory to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Explain how multiple layers of convolutions allow a device to 'see' abstract features like shapes, then textures, and finally objects.
sections.example: A smart camera on a delivery drone: early layers detect lines, middle layers detect shapes like wheels, and final layers identify the delivery box.
